Judgment on Edom.</title> <div sID="gen21196" type="x-p"/> Another feature of Israel's prosperity; those who exulted over Israel's humiliation, shall themselves be a "prey." Already stated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.12-Ezek.25.14">Eze 25:12-14</reference>; properly repeated here in full detail, as a commentary on <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.28">Eze 34:28</reference>. The Israelites "shall be no more a prey"; but Edom, the type of their most bitter foes, shall be destroyed irrecoverably.<div eID="gen21196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21197" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11702"/><hi type="bold">2. Mount Seir--</hi>that is, Idumea (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.9">Ge 36:9</reference>). Singled out as badly pre-eminent in its bitterness against God's people, to represent all their enemies everywhere and in all ages. So in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.5">Is 34:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1-Isa.63.4">63:1-4</reference>, Edom, the region of the greatest enmity towards God's people, is the ideal scene of the final judgments of all God's foes. "Seir" means "shaggy," alluding to its rugged hills and forests. <div eID="gen21197" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11703"/><div sID="gen21198" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11703"/><hi type="bold">3. most desolate--</hi>literally, "desolation and desolateness" (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.17">Jr 49:17</reference>, &c.). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11705"/><div sID="gen21203" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11705"/><hi type="bold">6. I will prepare thee unto blood--</hi>I will expose thee to slaughter.<div eID="gen21203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sith--</hi>old English for "seeing that" or "since."<div eID="gen21204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21205" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou hast not hated blood--</hi>The Hebrew order is, "thou hast hated not--blood"; that is, thou couldst not bear to live without bloodshed [Grotius]. There is a play on similar sounds in the Hebrew; Edom resembling dam, the Hebrew for "blood"; as "Edom" means "red," the transition to "blood" is easy. Edom, akin to blood in name, so also in nature and acts; "blood therefore shall pursue thee." The measure which Edom meted to others should be meted to himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.109.17">Psa 109:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.7.2">Mt 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.52">26:52</reference>). <div eID="gen21205" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 6. I will prepare thee unto blood-- I will expose thee to slaughter. sith-- old English for "seeing that" or "since." thou hast not hated blood-- The Hebrew order is, "thou hast hated not--blood"; that is, thou couldst not bear to live without bloodshed [Grotius]. There is a play on similar sounds in the Hebrew; Edom resembling dam, the Hebrew for "blood"; as "Edom" means "red," the transition to "blood" is easy. Edom, akin to blood in name, so also in nature and acts; "blood therefore shall pursue thee." The measure which Edom meted to others should be meted to himself ( Psa 109:17 ; Mt 7:2 ; 26:52 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11708"/><div sID="gen21208" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11708"/>10. So far from being allowed to enter on Israel's vacated inheritance, as Edom hoped (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.5">Eze 36:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.83.4">Psa 83:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.12">12</reference>; Ob 13), it shall be that he shall be deprived of his own; and whereas Israel's humiliation was temporary, Edom's shall be perpetual.<div eID="gen21208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21209" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord was there--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.35">Eze 48:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.1">Psa 48:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.48.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.132.13">132:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.14">14</reference>). Jehovah claimed Judea as His own, even when the Chaldeans had overthrown the state; they could not remove Him, as they did the idols of heathen lands. The broken sentences express the excited feelings of the prophet at Edom's wicked presumption. The transition from the "two nations and two countries" to "it" marks that the two are regarded as one whole. The last clause, "and Jehovah was there," bursts in, like a flash of lightning, reproving the wicked presumption of Edom's thought. <div eID="gen21209" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11710"/><div sID="gen21212" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11710"/><hi type="bold">12-13. blasphemies ... against ... Israel ... against me--</hi>God regards what is done against His people as done against Himself (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.45">Mt 25:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.9.2">Ac 9:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.4.5">4, 5</reference>). Edom implied, if he did not express it, in his taunts against Israel, that God had not sufficient power to protect His people. A type of the spirit of all the foes of God and His people (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.3">1Sa 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.6">Re 13:6</reference>). <div eID="gen21212" type="x-p"/>

Edom implied, if he did not express it, in his taunts against Israel, that God had not sufficient power to protect His people. A type of the spirit of all the foes of God and His people ( 1Sa 2:3 ; Re 13:6 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11711"/><div sID="gen21213" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11711"/>14. (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.13">Is 65:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.14">14</reference>). "The whole earth" refers to Judea and the nations that submit themselves to Judea's God; when these rejoice, the foes of God and His people, represented by Edom as a nation, shall be desolate. Things shall be completely reversed; Israel, that now for a time mourns, shall then rejoice and for ever. Edom, that now rejoices over fallen Israel, shall then, when elsewhere all is joy, mourn, and for ever (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.17-Isa.65.19">Is 65:17-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.5.4">Mt 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.25">Lu 6:25</reference>). Havernick loses this striking antithesis by translating, "According to the joy of the whole land (of Edom), so I will make thee desolate"; which would make <reference osisRef="Ezek.35.15">Eze 35:15</reference> a mere repetition of this. <div eID="gen21213" type="x-p"/>
